opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the uncertainty actually cuts in favor of working on it now rather than against it.

If you're unsure whether AI systems will be able to meaningfully automate research in five years or fifteen, you have to ask which mistake is worse. If capabilities arrive later than expected and we've invested heavily in alignment early, the cost is that some of that work turns out less relevant than we hoped. We'll have learned things and built tools, and the field will be more mature. If capabilities arrive sooner than expected and we haven't done the work, we're trying to figure out how to align very capable systems while they're already being deployed, under enormous commercial and competitive pressure. That asymmetry matters a lot.

The second reason is that a lot of alignment work has long lead times. Building good evaluations, developing interpretability techniques that actually scale, getting reliable methods for scalable oversight, and growing a community of researchers who know what they're doing all take years. You can't spin that up overnight once you notice a system is getting close to doing serious research on its own.

The third point is specific to the automated alignment researcher idea. One of the most promising paths, I think, is to use AI systems to help us do alignment research itself. But for that to work, we need to be able to trust the work those systems produce. We need ways to evaluate whether a proposed alignment technique is actually good, whether the system is being honest with us, and whether it's sandbagging or subtly steering things. Those evaluation and oversight problems are things we can work on right now with current models, and they get much harder to start on once the systems are smarter than us in the relevant domains.

Finally, current models are useful empirical testbeds. Ten years ago a lot of alignment work was necessarily theoretical, because we didn't have systems that exhibited the behaviors we cared about. Now we have models that can be deceptive in toy settings, that generalize in surprising ways, and that respond to training in ways we can study. That makes research much more tractable. I'd much rather be iterating on real systems now, while the stakes are relatively low, than waiting until the stakes are high and we're out of time to iterate.

So the uncertainty is real, but I don't think it's a reason to wait. It's a reason to start early and stay humble about which specific approaches will pay off.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we don't know how soon AI will be able to automate alignment research, and that's actually a big part of why I think it's worth working on now rather than waiting.

There are a few ways to see this. One is just the basic asymmetry. If it turns out that very capable systems are further away than some people think, then we've spent some time and talent on a problem that we would have had to solve eventually anyway, and we've built up a research community, tooling, and institutional know-how that will still be valuable when the time comes. That's not a terrible outcome. But if timelines are short and we haven't done the work, we could end up in a situation where we're deploying systems whose behavior we don't understand and can't reliably steer, and the cost of that could be enormous and hard to reverse. So under uncertainty, you want to be erring on the side of being prepared.

The second thing is that alignment research isn't just something you turn on when the problem becomes urgent. A lot of it is slow, cumulative work. You need people who have developed taste for which problems matter, you need empirical results that tell you which techniques actually hold up as models get more capable, and you need to find out where your current ideas break. We learned a lot from doing RLHF at scale that we wouldn't have figured out from the whiteboard. The same is true for things like scalable oversight or interpretability. If you only start when the stakes are obviously high, you're starting from scratch at the worst possible moment.

And then the third point, which I think is maybe the most important, is about the automation question itself. I'm actually fairly optimistic that AI systems will be able to do a lot of alignment research for us at some point. That's been a big part of how I think about the long-term strategy. But getting there safely is itself an alignment problem. To trust a model to help you align the next model, you need to be able to oversee it, verify its work, and be confident it isn't subtly steering you wrong. That capability doesn't fall out of the sky. We need to build the techniques now that would let us actually use AI assistance for this, and we need to figure out how much we can trust it and in what domains. So the possibility of automating alignment research isn't an argument for waiting. It's an argument for doing the groundwork so that when the systems are capable enough, we're in a position to use them well.

I'd also just add that right now is a pretty good time to be doing this empirically. The models are capable enough that many of the problems people used to speculate about are becoming concrete and testable, but they're not yet so capable that mistakes are catastrophic. That window won't last forever, and I think we should use it.

astra-6.text:
I think uncertainty about when AI can automate research is itself a reason to work on alignment now. We need a strategy that works across a range of timelines. If that capability comes soon, we’ll want to have made enough progress that we can actually use it safely. And if it takes longer, the research we do in the meantime could be really important.

There’s also a distinction between an AI that can do useful research and an AI whose research you can trust. If we ask a system to help us align its successor, how do we evaluate its proposals? How do we know it hasn’t found something that looks good to us but fails in a situation we didn’t test? Automating research doesn’t automatically solve those problems.

So part of the work now is figuring out what we would want to delegate, how we would supervise it, and what evidence would give us confidence in the result. You don’t need to believe humans will solve the whole alignment problem unaided to think that getting that process started is very valuable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think uncertainty about the timeline is itself a reason to work on alignment now. We don’t know how much time we have, and there are important questions we can already study with current systems: how to supervise behavior that’s difficult for humans to evaluate, how to tell whether a model is actually doing what we want, and how to make our methods work as models become more capable.

AI automating research could be enormously helpful. But then you face the question: can you trust the research it’s doing? If we want to use AI to help solve alignment, we need enough alignment already to make that assistance reliable. So I see the work we do now as laying the groundwork for that, as well as giving us a better chance of being prepared if progress is fast.
